title: Magnets: Stick or Not?
description: Magnets pull some things and ignore others completely. Which materials stick, which never will, and the invisible force field doing the pulling.

body.heading: The invisible pull
paragraphs: A magnet has a superpower you cannot see: it pulls certain metals toward itself, right through air, paper, even your hand. Scientists call the pulling area around it a magnetic field. You cannot see the field — but you can watch it work.
The strange part? Magnets are picky. Some things leap to a magnet. Others sit there as if nothing happened. Knowing which is which is the whole game.

body.heading: It sticks!
paragraphs: Things made of iron and steel stick to magnets: paper clips, nails, screws, keys, most coins' cousins the steel washers, fridge doors, scissors, and the metal strip on a toolbox.
If a magnet could talk to a paper clip across the table, the paper clip would come sliding over to say hello. That sliding is the field at work.

body.heading: It never sticks
paragraphs: Wood, plastic, paper, rubber, glass, cloth, leaves, stones and your fingers: a magnet ignores them all, forever, no matter how strong it is.
And here is the trick that fools everyone: not all metals stick either. Aluminum cans and most gold, silver and copper say no thank you. Magnets mainly love iron and steel.

body.heading: Two magnets: push and pull
paragraphs: Every magnet has two ends called poles. Bring two magnets together one way and they pull (attract). Flip one around and they push apart (repel) — you can feel an invisible cushion between them, like two hands pressing.
That push is how some fast trains float above their tracks — magnets repelling magnets, lifting tons of train on an invisible cushion.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Predict before you test: will a magnet stick to a bathtub? A bicycle? A banana? A bookshelf screw? Write your guesses, then check with a grown-up.
2. Why do you think 'stick or not?' is a better science question than just 'does it stick?' — what does the NOT teach us?

takeaway: Magnets pull iron and steel through an invisible field, ignore wood, plastic and even some metals like aluminum — and two magnets can push as well as pull.
materials: Just this page to read — or, to try it: one ordinary fridge magnet and a grown-up to hunt with
supervision: A grown-up joins the optional magnet hunt, especially around small objects.
safetyNotes: Small magnets and small metal objects are choking hazards for children under 3 — keep them away from toddlers and never put magnets in mouths.
Strong or toy magnets with small parts: if two magnets are ever swallowed they are a medical emergency — tell a grown-up immediately and see a doctor.
Keep magnets away from phones, bank cards and computers, which they can damage; and never use anything electrical for this experiment.
screenFreeExtension: Magnet hunt at home with a grown-up: predict 'stick or not' for ten objects, test each with a fridge magnet, and score your predictions.
